question: One of these libraries resolves references to things that live outside its own data - an identifier that has to be turned into something fetchable, and remote documents that have to be pulled in before a result can be produced. Resolution has three possible outcomes, not two: it succeeded, it has not finished yet, and it failed. Throughout this library only the first two are modelled, and the third is quietly folded into one of them, in four different places and four different ways. A shared bounded store keyed by location keeps whatever the last attempt produced, including the placeholder that means "this attempt failed", and the store has no operation for forgetting an entry at all, so one bad moment on the network makes that location permanently unavailable for the rest of the session; a second surface keeps a per-object promise for the same reason and never discards the rejected one, so a retry can never happen. A third place keeps showing what the previous reference resolved to after the reference itself is changed or taken away, because it only reacts when the resolved end product differs, and the end product of "nothing" is not something it compares. A fourth treats a reference that cannot currently be resolved as a reference that does not exist: it is dropped from the material handed to the next consumer rather than carried across unresolved, and an error raised while removing one is swallowed so the caller believes the removal happened. Each of these is invisible whenever the network cooperates and whenever references are only ever added. The contract is that a failed resolution is a transient fact about one attempt, never a value to be stored in place of the thing, and that a reference whose target cannot be produced right now must be kept, retried and reported rather than substituted with absence. Elsewhere in the folder that separation is the design: one library gives a failing attempt its own object with its own lifecycle - it can be paused, resumed, cancelled and asked for its status, and its failure never becomes the stored value - and another enumerates the three outcomes explicitly as distinct states so that a failure travels alongside the data rather than replacing it. Which files store, keep or discard a failed resolution as though it were an answer, and which own the contract they have to be brought in line with?

anchor.pr_title: fix(editor): export embedding of multi-url styles, font lists, failed fetches and bare @import rules

grader_notes.why_cross_repo: ANCHOR: four independent post-pin tldraw fixes, all mined from `pin..origin/main`, pin-is-ancestor True, all removed-line verified live at the pin 5590d14d8e. (1) #10338 (4651ebb3ac) - fetchCache.ts memoises the promise for every url INCLUDING the `null` it returns on a failed fetch, and LruCache.ts at the pin has no `delete` at all, so the cache structurally cannot forget a poisoned entry; the fix adds `LruCache.delete` and evicts null results, and repairs FontEmbedder.ts / StyleEmbedder.ts / parseCss.ts, which consume those cached nulls (9/9, 3/3, 2/2 removed lines live). (2) #10226 (f35842e3ba) - ImageShapeUtil.tsx / VideoShapeUtil.tsx memoise the export promise per shape and keep it after rejection, so a failed export can never be retried (6/6, 1/1 live). (3) #10250 (5be37f92cb) - useImageOrVideoAsset.ts returns early when assetId is falsy without clearing the previous result, and skips resolution whenever the resolved url equals `previousUrl`, so a removed, re-attached or same-url asset keeps the stale render (3/3 live). (4) #10208 (46368b7754) - BookmarkShapeUtil.tsx / bookmarks.ts only act when the resolved asset differs, so changing a bookmark's url leaves the old asset (5/5, 11/11 live). (5) #10366 + #10368 (e22dbf6261, b10f608cba) - Editor.ts drops assets it cannot resolve from copied content and swallows asset-store removal errors (10/10 and 1/1 live). calibration.note: Designed as hard and measured medium. The bare arm found the whole export/cache half of the gold (fetchCache.ts, LruCache.ts, FontEmbedder.ts, StyleEmbedder.ts, ImageShapeUtil.tsx, VideoShapeUtil.tsx, useImageOrVideoAsset.ts, Editor.ts, plus both citations) by grepping for caches and export code: 'cache' is the contract's own mechanism and it is spelled in the file names. It missed exactly the three members whose subject matter is unrelated to the contract's vocabulary - bookmarks.ts, BookmarkShapeUtil.tsx and parseCss.ts. Design lesson for the next attempt: a contract whose MECHANISM is nameable (a cache, an export pipeline) is greppable even when no single identifier reaches a majority of gold; the greppability screen on identifiers does not catch it.
